## Why This Is Asked
Guardrails for input data ensure predictable plans and reduce drift due to outside changes.

## Key Concepts
- Terraform variable validation blocks
- contains and range checks via logical expressions
- error_message behavior on plan/apply
- user experience when invalid inputs are provided

## Code Example
```
variable "instance_count" {
  type = number
  validation {
    condition = var.instance_count >= 1 && var.instance_count <= 5
    error_message = "instance_count must be between 1 and 5."
  }
}

variable "region" {
  type = string
  validation {
    condition = contains(["us-east-1", "us-west-2", "eu-west-1"], var.region)
    error_message = "region must be one of us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1."
  }
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend validation to a list of allowed instance_types?
- How would you provide user-friendly error messages for multiple invalid variables?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to onboard existing resources into Terraform without affecting production, using a minimal module and proper backend initialization.

## Key Concepts
- Terraform module scaffolding for existing resources
- Backend initialization with environment-specific state keys
- `terraform import` for bringing existing resources into state
- Plan validation and CI gating to prevent accidental applies

## Code Example
```hcl
# modules/iam/main.tf
resource "aws_iam_role" "this" {
  name               = var.name
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.assume.json
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "assume" {
  statement {
    effect = "Allow"
    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["ec2.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    actions = ["sts:AssumeRole"]
  }
}

# modules/bucket/main.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "this" {
  bucket = var.bucket_name
}

# environments/dev/main.tf
module "iam" {
  source = "../../modules/iam"
  name   = "existing-role-name"
}

module "bucket" {
  source      = "../../modules/bucket"
  bucket_name = "existing-bucket-name"
}
```

## Minimal CI Gating Snippet
```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Run import and plan
export TF_VAR_name="existing-role-name"
export TF_VAR_bucket_name="existing-bucket-name"

terraform init -backend-config="key=envs/dev/terraform.tfstate"
terraform import module.iam.aws_iam_role.this arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/existing-role
terraform import module.bucket.aws_s3_bucket.this existing-bucket-name

# Verify no drift before allowing apply
terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
if grep -q "No changes" plan.tfplan; then
    echo "Import verified - no drift detected"
    terraform apply plan.tfplan
else
    echo "ERROR: Drift detected after import. Review plan output."
    exit 1
fi
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to isolate a canary environment from prod using backend aliasing, workspace management, and CI gates, ensuring no inadvertent prod drift. It also exercises JSON plan parsing and gating, which scales to many environments.

## Key Concepts
- Backend aliasing for per-env state
- Terraform workspaces for isolated planning
- terraform plan output as JSON for policy checks
- CI gating and manual approvals to control applies

## Code Example
```javascript
# Backend setup
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=tfstate" \
  -backend-config="key=envs/canary/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=us-east-1" \
  -backend-config="dynamodb_table=tf-locks"

# Canary setup
terraform workspace new canary
terraform plan -out=canary.plan
terraform show -json canary.plan > canary.json

# Validate all addresses are within canary and no prod addresses
```
